title: Go Big Or Go Home

jokes.text: Leslie bursts into the office yelling 'Giddyup! Giddyup!' and declares 'I am the pants queen!'
jokes.setup: Cold open presents Leslie as a competent government employee
jokes.punchline: She immediately undermines professional gravitas by galloping in like a horse and crowning herself 'pants queen'
jokes.explanation: Works well as a character establishment beat — Leslie's unchecked enthusiasm expressed through absurd royal self-proclamation is very on-brand. The specific absurdity of 'pants queen' is funnier than a generic exclamation. Not a top-tier joke but a strong opener that sets the season's tone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Pants queen!

jokes.text: April's talking-head: 'My mom is Puerto Rican. That's why I'm so lively and colorful.'
jokes.setup: The mockumentary intro presents each character with a flattering descriptor
jokes.punchline: April — famously stone-faced and nihilistic — claims Puerto Rican heritage makes her 'lively and colorful,' delivered completely deadpan
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The entire comedy is predicated on the audience knowing April is the least lively and colorful person in Pawnee. The self-description is the exact opposite of her personality, delivered with her signature deadpan. Near-perfect character integration — no other character on any show could land this joke. Economy is pristine: one sentence does all the work. Earns its 8+ because the gap between the claim and the character's reality is both funny and a little subversive regarding ethnic stereotyping.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Tom, you have to stop doing that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But Leslie, I enjoy annoying you. It's like my favorite hobby. Well, that and online shopping for things I don't need.

jokes.text: Tom calls himself 'Tommy Timberlake' and sings it to himself
jokes.setup: The intro narration announces Tom Haverford
jokes.punchline: Tom has apparently rebranded himself as 'Tommy Timberlake' and is singing his own name to the tune of a Justin Timberlake song
jokes.explanation: Solid Tom moment — his celebrity worship and desire to rebrand himself is a core character trait. The joke is efficient and character-specific. Not especially original but executed well within the format.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm Tommy Timberlake!

jokes.text: Ben's talking-head: 'Scientists believe that the first human being who will live 150 years has already been born. I believe I am that human being.'
jokes.setup: Chris is introduced as someone who brought 'disturbing news'
jokes.punchline: Before delivering the bad news, Chris non-sequiturs into his belief that he is literally the immortal human being scientists predict will live 150 years — delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: A tremendous character introduction joke. Chris's delusional optimism and physical self-obsession are encapsulated perfectly. Starting from a real scientific claim and then having him personally identify as the chosen one is an inspired escalation. The sincerity of delivery is everything. Highly quotable, earns 8+ because the concept is genuinely original and perfectly character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I have the same dead, expressionless stare and general apathy that I've had since childhood. I'm not sure why. I think it started when I was born and the doctor slapped me, and I thought, 'okay, whatever.'

jokes.text: Ron's response to Leslie announcing they're back: 'Bully.'
jokes.setup: Leslie excitedly announces the return to work after a long furlough
jokes.punchline: Ron responds with the single word 'Bully' — an archaic term of approval — communicating absolute contentment at maximum verbal economy
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Swansonian. One word conveys his entire personality: old-fashioned, minimal, satisfied. Economy score is nearly perfect — you could not do this in fewer words. The archaic word choice (Teddy Roosevelt-era slang) does double duty characterizing Ron's values. Strong joke, though not a showstopper.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Nailed it.

jokes.text: Leslie throws Jerry's puzzle into a fountain to signal the end of his leisure time
jokes.setup: Leslie visits Jerry, who has been enjoying retirement-style activities during the furlough with a puzzle
jokes.punchline: Leslie declares 'The nightmare's over' and without hesitation throws his puzzle into a fountain. Jerry's 'Come on!' is the perfect helpless reaction.
jokes.explanation: A physical gag that neatly encapsulates both Leslie's relentless energy and Jerry's status as the group's punching bag. The 'Come on!' is perfectly helpless. The puzzle detail is a nice specific touch — not just something being thrown. Functional, crowd-pleasing slapstick.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I've been training my body like a machine. I do 200 sit-ups every morning, I only eat foods that are genetically similar to foods that humans ate 10,000 years ago, and I've eliminated all processed sugars and refined carbohydrates from my diet. So when this shutdown is over, I'll still be here. In fact, I'll probably live to be 150 years old.

jokes.text: Andy shouts 'I called shotgun! Everybody heard me!' in the car
jokes.setup: The team is heading back to work; context suggests Andy is in the back seat despite calling shotgun
jokes.punchline: Andy's indignant, childlike insistence on shotgun protocol — appealing to witnesses — is perfectly on-character for a man-child
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, totally in character for Andy. The idea of Andy appealing to 'everybody' as witnesses to his shotgun call is a small gem of childish logic. Works well as a quick transition beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We're back to work!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Dear God, no.

jokes.text: Ron's 'speech': 'Well, I am usually not one for speeches. So, goodbye.'
jokes.setup: Ron appears to be about to give a welcome-back speech to the team
jokes.punchline: He immediately subverts the expectation by declaring his distaste for speeches and sitting down after a single word
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is flawless: the setup ('I am usually not one for speeches') creates an expectation that a speech is coming anyway — the punchline ('So, goodbye.') is the exact opposite of what the form demands. Maximum economy: 12 words that do the work of a soliloquy. Near-perfect character integration because only Ron Swanson's anti-government, anti-sentiment worldview makes this joke land. Genuinely quotable and endlessly rewatchable. Earns 8.6 — comparable to the anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: All work activities have been suspended: no meetings, no emails, no reports, no committees.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is paradise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is torture.

jokes.text: Tom's speech ends with 'Break's over, mofos.'
jokes.setup: After Ron's ultra-minimal speech, Tom steps up as if to give a more energetic address
jokes.punchline: Tom's entire 'inspirational' return-to-work speech is the single sentence 'Break's over, mofos'
jokes.explanation: Funny as a contrast after Ron's 'goodbye,' but this is the weaker of the two minimal-speech jokes. Tom's vernacular is on-brand but the joke is less precisely constructed than Ron's.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Feel my goose bumps! Feel them!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, just feel them. This is how excited I am to be back at work.

jokes.text: Leslie redirects team from pizza to saving the parks; Andy counters 'Fine, but after that, the pizza is our top priority.' Leslie: 'No, it's not.' Andy: 'We're getting pizza?'
jokes.setup: Leslie rallies the team to 'make this town fun,' rebuking Andy's 'make the world's biggest pizza' suggestion
jokes.punchline: Andy concedes the pizza plan but immediately tries to re-insert it as 'top priority after' the real mission; when denied, he hears only that pizza is still happening
jokes.explanation: A two-part joke that escalates nicely. Andy's negotiating tactic of making pizza 'top priority AFTER' the real work is clever character writing. The final 'We're getting pizza?' perfectly captures Andy's selective comprehension. Both beats land well and the rhythm is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Love is like finding the perfect pair of shoes. You search and search, and when you finally find them, they fit just right.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: That's actually really sweet, Tom.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I tried those shoes on you and they don't fit. You got hippo feet.

jokes.text: Andy's voicemail to April: 'This is like the 200th message I've left you, without a response. So, if you're trying to tell me something, I do not know what it is because you won't call me back.'
jokes.setup: Andy is leaving yet another voicemail for April after she disappeared
jokes.punchline: After establishing he's left 200 unanswered messages, Andy genuinely cannot parse the obvious signal that April is ignoring him
jokes.explanation: The joke hinges on Andy's lovable obliviousness — 200 unanswered messages and he still can't figure out the signal. The escalation (200 messages) followed by the sincere puzzlement is a strong structural choice. The phrasing 'if you're trying to tell me something, I do not know what it is' is both the joke and a perfect character beat. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: HEY JEREMY, YOU SUCK!

jokes.text: Ben explains the reason basketball must be funded: 'In Indiana, if you don't provide a basketball league, people get very upset. And quite frankly, throw things at you and call you names. Like Turd-boy. Whatever.'
jokes.setup: Ben is delivering the bureaucratic bad news about budget cuts
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'upset' to 'throw things' to 'call you names' to the specific example 'Turd-boy' is perfectly deadpan; the 'Whatever' dismissal at the end suggests this has happened to Ben personally
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'Turd-boy' and the casual 'Whatever' make this a strong joke. The escalation from bureaucratic language to childish name-calling is a great structural contrast. The implication that Ben himself has been called Turd-boy adds a layer. Economy is good — doesn't overstay its welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? Sports bras are genius. We should make a sports bra for men.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, no. We should make sports bras for dogs. Think about it—dogs running around, their nipples bouncing everywhere.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But here's where it gets good. We make the bras out of rubber. Rubber nipples. For when the dogs want to feel... protected.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We call it 'Pup Armor.' I'm telling you, this is the next big thing. We'll be millionaires.

jokes.text: Ron's speech to basketball kids: 'Under my tutelage, you will grow from boys into men, from men into gladiators, and from gladiators into Swansons.'
jokes.setup: Ron addresses his youth basketball team with apparent gravitas
jokes.punchline: The climactic escalation (boys → men → gladiators) arrives at the absurdly self-aggrandizing destination of 'Swansons' — as if 'Swanson' is a category of being above gladiator
jokes.explanation: This is the standout line of the episode. The escalating three-part structure (boys → men → gladiators) is a classical rhetorical device that sets an expectation of noble aspiration — then crashes into Ron's narcissism by making 'Swanson' the apex of human achievement. The joke works on multiple levels: it's absurd, it's perfectly character-specific, and the escalation structure is elegant. 'Swansons' as a plural category of super-gladiators is inspired. Highly quotable and endlessly rewatchable. Earns 8.7.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The nightmare is over!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I threw it in the water.

jokes.text: Ron unveils 'The Swanson Pyramid of Greatness' — a giant laminated poster he has apparently been developing for years
jokes.setup: Ron dramatically announces 'Behold!' after his speech
jokes.punchline: He reveals a professionally produced pyramid chart of life philosophies he has spent years developing — for personal use, now deployed on youth basketball children
jokes.explanation: The visual gag of Ron having a laminated, multi-year project called 'The Swanson Pyramid of Greatness' is excellent. The effort and formality of the artifact — deployed on small children for basketball — is the core comedy. Strong rewatch value because the pyramid itself contains many jokes within it.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I called shotgun.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That was like three hours ago.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Shotgun doesn't expire. It's like a gift card to the front seat.

jokes.text: Pyramid category: 'Capitalism. God's way of determining who is smart, and who is poor.'
jokes.setup: Ron reads from the Pyramid of Greatness categories
jokes.punchline: Capitalism is defined as a divine sorting mechanism between the intelligent and the poor — presented as self-evident wisdom
jokes.explanation: A sharply written one-liner that distills Ron's Libertarian worldview to its most extreme, unapologetic form. The phrase 'God's way of determining who is smart, and who is poor' has a nice rhythm and the casual equation of poverty with lack of intelligence is darkly funny and politically pointed. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have something to say.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Goodbye.

jokes.text: Pyramid category: 'Crying. Acceptable at funerals and the Grand Canyon.'
jokes.setup: Continuing to read Pyramid of Greatness categories
jokes.punchline: Crying is deemed acceptable in only two specific, very different contexts — one solemn (funerals), one scenic (Grand Canyon)
jokes.explanation: The unexpected pairing of 'funerals' and 'the Grand Canyon' as the only two acceptable crying situations is wonderfully absurd. The Grand Canyon's inclusion implies Ron has in fact cried there — a tiny revelation about his hidden emotional depth. Extremely economical. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know, I really believe in each and every one of you. Together, we can accomplish anything we set our minds to.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's great, Leslie. Hey, did anyone else hear that? I think someone just ordered pizza in the break room.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, I'm trying to inspire the team here.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, I know, but is it pepperoni? Because if it's pepperoni, I need to be there right now.

jokes.text: Pyramid category: 'Fish, for sport only, not for meat. Fish meat is practically a vegetable.'
jokes.setup: Continuing Pyramid categories
jokes.punchline: Ron's contempt for fish as food is codified into a moral principle; his reasoning that fish meat 'is practically a vegetable' is bizarre but delivered as settled science
jokes.explanation: The logical leap that fish meat equals vegetable is charmingly absurd and consistent with Ron's meat-purist philosophy. The category structure (sport only, not for meat) suggests he has given this serious policy consideration. Works well as a Pyramid entry.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey April, it's Andy. I was just thinking about you and I wanted to call and see what you're up to. Maybe we could hang out sometime? Like, I don't know, get some food or something? Anyway, just let me know. I'm pretty free most nights. Okay, bye!

jokes.text: Ron examines a child's haircut: 'Are the scissors broken in your house, son?'
jokes.setup: Ron reads the haircut category (only three acceptable cuts) and surveys his players
jokes.punchline: He addresses a child whose hair is presumably long or unconventional with the withering, deadpan question about broken scissors
jokes.explanation: A deadpan zinger that is all the funnier for being directed at a child. The framing as a practical inquiry ('are the scissors broken?') rather than an insult is characteristic of Ron's oblivious certainty. Economical and quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm going to be very clear about what you can and cannot do in this position.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! Go Jerry!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? I haven't even started yet.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, I'm just getting ahead of it. That's my guy right there!

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'I'm not a paper pusher, Ann. I need to be out in the streets, planting trees and cracking skulls.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is venting about the slashed budget and her frustration at being underutilized
jokes.punchline: The passionate civic mission of 'planting trees' is paired with the incongruously violent 'cracking skulls' as if both are equal parts of the Parks job description
jokes.explanation: A gem of a line. The juxtaposition of wholesome civic activity with mob-boss violence is very funny, and Leslie delivers it as if both are equivalent parts of her job. The rhythm ('planting trees AND cracking skulls') is excellent. Strong quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was called 'Turd-boy' in middle school. For three years. Do you know what that does to a person? That's why we need this basketball league.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Is there anything we can do about that?' Ben: 'No.' Chris: 'Damn! Sorry, Leslie.'
jokes.setup: Chris asks if there's anything they can do about the slashed programs, apparently hoping for a yes
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately says no; Chris's exasperated 'Damn!' followed by a polite apology to Leslie captures both his enthusiasm and his impotence
jokes.explanation: A quick, effective exchange. Chris's boundless positivity crashing into bureaucratic reality ('Damn!') and then his immediate pivot to politeness is a good character beat. Ben's one-word 'No' is perfectly dry. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have nothing but respect for basketball players. You're strong, you're disciplined, and you understand the importance of hard work. That's why I'm here today to propose something radical: we change your team name from the Sweetbriar Slugs to something with real power and dignity. The Swansons.

jokes.text: Leslie confronts Chris about not having faith in her department; he says 'Fair enough. Go the other way.' Leslie tries to exit but is going the wrong way; they awkwardly redirect each other.
jokes.setup: Leslie storms off after confronting Chris
jokes.punchline: She's going the wrong direction; Chris's 'Go the other way' and her stubborn attempt to continue creates a brief physical comedy beat
jokes.explanation: A minor physical comedy beat that deflates the tension of the confrontation. Competent but generic — the 'wrong direction exit' gag is a common sitcom move. Does nothing special with the characters. Low quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I present to you the Ron Swanson Pyramid of Greatness. Each level represents a different aspect of greatness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: At the base, we have capitalism. The engine of achievement.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Next, we have honor, integrity, and good scotch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: At the top, we have me.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ann debate whether Chris is hot vs. intense vs. their boss: 'He's very... He's pretty hot.' 'Yeah, he's hot. But he's intense. But he's really, really hot. But he's your boss.'
jokes.setup: Ann turns down Chris; Leslie asks about it after
jokes.punchline: The two friends cycle through pros and cons but keep returning to 'but he's really, really hot' as if his attractiveness overwhelms all other considerations
jokes.explanation: The rapid-fire tennis match of 'hot but intense but hot but boss' has good rhythm and is relatable. Not particularly original but executed with good timing. The escalating 'really, really hot' is the payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: There are three ways to accomplish something: the right way, the wrong way, and the way that I do it.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Capitalism: God's way of determining who is smart and who is poor.

jokes.text: Leslie's 'idea' to save the Parks Department: 'Would you be cool doing things that a prostitute does? Minus the money?'
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she just thought of a great idea to save the department and asks Ann a leading question
jokes.punchline: The question — which is asking Ann to seduce Chris for budget information — is framed in the most alarming way possible ('things a prostitute does, minus the money')
jokes.explanation: A very well-structured joke. The setup (Leslie has an idea) leads to an alarming question that the audience processes as potentially sexual, then Ann's 'Definitely yes, then. Thanks, Ann' and Leslie's exit before explaining makes the prostitute comparison the entire visible comedy. The 'minus the money' specification is a perfect detail. Strong structure and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: There are only three acceptable times for a man to cry: when he's chpping onions, when he's watching the great films, and when a trout bites his hand off.

jokes.text: Ann: 'Definitely yes, then. Thanks, Ann.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just asked Ann to do 'what a prostitute does, minus the money'
jokes.punchline: Ann immediately agrees ('Definitely yes, then'), and Leslie thanks herself ('Thanks, Ann') before Ann can process what she agreed to
jokes.explanation: The button on joke 24. Leslie's 'Thanks, Ann' — thanking her friend before Ann has even fully processed — is a great Leslie moment: she's already moved on to implementation. Quick, efficient, good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Fish are vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: They don't have legs, so they can't run away. That means they're vegetables.

jokes.text: Andy's coaching philosophy talking-head: 'I'd say my coaching style is centered around fundamentals, with an emphasis on fun. And a second emphasis on mental.'
jokes.setup: Andy describes his approach to coaching youth basketball
jokes.punchline: Andy realizes mid-sentence that 'fun' and 'mental' combine to spell 'fundamental' — he didn't plan this, he's just noticing it as he speaks
jokes.explanation: An excellent bit. The accidental wordplay on 'fundamentals' broken into 'fun' and 'mental' is the joke — Andy is discovering his own insight in real time, which is perfect character writing. The 'second emphasis on mental' reads as either sinister or genuinely proud of the discovery. High character integration because this can only happen with Andy's particular brand of accidental self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Your hair looks like a bird's nest made of disappointment and broken dreams.

jokes.text: Andy's talking-head about coaching: 'But every time I look one of these kids in the eyes and he calls me Coach... That's how I know I agreed to be a coach.'
jokes.setup: Andy appears to be building to a heartfelt statement about what coaching means to him
jokes.punchline: The expected emotional payoff ('that's how I know it's all worth it / I made a difference') is replaced by the tautological 'that's how I know I agreed to be a coach' — Andy's deepest insight is just confirmation of a fact
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliantly constructed misdirection. The camera setup, the pause, and the earnest tone create every expectation of a heartwarming coach-movie speech. The subversion — that the moment only confirms the established fact that he is a coach — is both absurd and perfectly Andy. Structure is near-perfect. The tautological punchline has a specific kind of genius: it could only come from a character who is sincere but not particularly reflective. Earns 8.3.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe we have to cut the budget again. This is absolutely ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Son of a b—

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I apologize. That was inappropriate.

jokes.text: Tom announces 'Match point. Touchdown. Et cetera.' to start the basketball game
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to do the coin toss / official game opening
jokes.punchline: Tom uses completely wrong sports terminology to begin a basketball game, listing several wrong terms and finishing with the dismissive 'et cetera'
jokes.explanation: The 'et cetera' is the best part — Tom can't be bothered to continue listing wrong terms and just gestures at all the other ones he doesn't know. Efficient and character-consistent. The coin toss in basketball joke from Ron immediately before adds to it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I work hard. I play hard. I give everything 110%. And when someone gets in my way, I crack skulls.

jokes.text: Tom: 'Are those women's sneakers?' Andy: 'Yes, they are, Ron. You know what? They fit better, I got an employee discount, and the best part is no one can tell.'
jokes.setup: Andy arrives to coach in unusual footwear
jokes.punchline: Andy confirms they are women's sneakers and offers three rationalizations, ending with 'no one can tell' — which is clearly not true since Tom just noticed immediately
jokes.explanation: Andy's complete unselfconsciousness is the joke — he doesn't realize 'no one can tell' is already disproven by the fact that Tom noticed. The three-reason justification (fits better, discount, no one can tell) is a good comic structure where each reason is slightly worse than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Well, we could always try to get a grant, or maybe reallocate some funds from another department. There are actually several options we could explore that might—

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, I got excited about budget solutions for a second there. That was inappropriate.

jokes.text: Tom is coaching girls with instructions: 'I like what you're wearing, but I need it to be 300% sexier. Do you have any of those shirts that look wet all the time? Or, like, a metal bikini?'
jokes.setup: Tom is ostensibly coaching the cheerleaders/sideline girls
jokes.punchline: Tom's coaching advice is entirely about sexiness of outfit — specifically requesting 'shirts that look wet all the time' and 'a metal bikini' — delivered with coaching sincerity
jokes.explanation: Tom's sleazy shallow superficiality expressed through 'coaching' advice is character-specific. The 'metal bikini' reference (Star Wars: Return of the Jedi) adds a nerdy layer. 'Shirts that look wet all the time' is a specific, genuinely funny absurd detail.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris, I can't believe you're not supporting me on this initiative!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Leslie, I am supporting you, I'm just trying to be fiscally responsible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if you moved out of my way, I could actually get somewhere!

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm trying to move! You keep going the same direction I'm going!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you keep blocking me!

jokes.text: Tom's coaching advice on sexy food: 'You know what's always sexy? Fingerless gloves.' / 'Turkey chili.'
jokes.setup: Tom is advising on how to look sexy; the girl asks about a 'normal, sane outfit' and Tom pivots to 'sexy food'
jokes.punchline: Tom suggests fingerless gloves as universally sexy, then — after asparagus is rejected — lands on 'turkey chili' as the sexy food
jokes.explanation: The journey from 'fingerless gloves' to 'turkey chili' as erotic touchstones is charmingly absurd. 'Turkey chili' as the summit of sensuality is unexpected and specific — the specificity (not just 'chili,' but turkey chili) is what elevates it slightly.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Why won't you go out with me?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Chris, that kiss was like kissing a tall, blond, athletic who's-who of disappointment. Your mouth tasted like you'd been eating a tire fire. And when you tried to grab my butt, you missed and got my hip. I've never felt less attractive in my entire life.

jokes.text: Leslie role-plays as Chris to show Ann how to steer a date conversation toward the Parks budget; as 'Chris' she opens her vest seductively and says 'Just like the budget needs to pop open and you need to pour it into my Parks Department.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is coaching Ann on how to subtly work the budget topic into a romantic date with Chris
jokes.punchline: Leslie's demonstration abandons all subtlety and has her dramatically opening her vest with a sexual metaphor about the budget being 'poured into' the Parks Department
jokes.explanation: Leslie's total inability to be subtle — even when demonstrating subtlety — is a great character joke. The vest-popping-budget-pouring metaphor is a bizarre sexual-political mashup that only Leslie would construct and consider effective. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So you're saying you would do all those things... just not for money?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Yes! Absolutely!

jokes.text: Chris on the date: 'I have never had a bad date. They've all been either great or phenomenally great.'
jokes.setup: Chris is enthusiastically describing how much he loves dates
jokes.punchline: The spectrum of his date quality runs only from 'great' to 'phenomenally great' — he has literally no frame of reference for a bad date
jokes.explanation: A clean bit that perfectly encapsulates Chris's unrealistic positivity. The binary of 'great or phenomenally great' with no lower option is funny and becomes a setup for his later revelation that this date IS his first bad date. Gains a callback bonus in retrospect.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, my coaching philosophy is all about building character and teaching kids the fundamentals of the game.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's not about winning, it's about the journey.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Watch this.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Hey kids, go get it!

jokes.text: Chris on dates: 'I have never had a bad date. They've all been either great or phenomenally great.'
jokes.setup: Chris is expressing enthusiasm for the date
jokes.punchline: He has no scale for bad dates — his spectrum runs from 'great' to 'phenomenally great,' eliminating the possibility of failure
jokes.explanation: Chris's positivity so complete that his categorical spectrum excludes the negative. Good character consistency. Sets up the payoff later when this is subverted.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, being a coach has really changed my life. I wake up every morning and I think about all these kids looking up to me, depending on me to guide them, to shape their futures. And I realize that I have this incredible responsibility to be someone they can believe in, someone they can trust, someone who—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, how do I know I'm a coach?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The kids call me Coach.

jokes.text: Chris tells Ann: 'Nurses are the most undervalued members of our society by far. I think all of you should make as much money as the CEO of Google.'
jokes.setup: Chris is trying to impress Ann on their date by praising her profession
jokes.punchline: Chris advocates not just for fair pay but that all nurses should make as much as the CEO of Google — a wildly impractical benchmark delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: The 'CEO of Google' as the specific benchmark for nurse salaries is funny — Chris doesn't say 'a fair wage' or even 'doctors' money,' he skips to the very top of the economic ladder. The sincerity sells it. Competent character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Are those women's sneakers?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: They are, but hear me out. Women's sneakers are designed with a narrower heel and a more tapered toe box. Plus, they come in way better colors and patterns. And they're often cheaper. So I get superior comfort and style at a lower price point. It's just smart shopping. And honestly, no one can tell.

jokes.text: Chris explains his positivity: 'I was born with a blood disorder. And my parents were told that I had three weeks to live. And here I still am, some 2,000-odd weeks later, and I have enjoyed every one of them.'
jokes.setup: Ann asks why Chris is so positive all the time
jokes.punchline: Chris's backstory (terminal diagnosis as a baby, still alive) is delivered matter-of-factly; the math of '2,000-odd weeks' (about 38 years) converting a life into weeks is both funny and charming
jokes.explanation: A very effective character revelation joke. Counting life in weeks rather than years is an unusual choice that reinforces his obsessive tracking of his own health. The casual delivery of a potentially tragic backstory as cheerful explanation is perfectly Chris. Also provides genuine character depth while being funny.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Alright everyone, let's get this basketball game started. First we need to do the coin toss, or whatever—the thing where you throw the ball up and people jump for it. Then we run back and forth, and try to put the ball in the hoop. There's a guy with a whistle. And at the end, whoever has the most points wins, obviously. And then there's... timeouts, and fouls, and traveling, and the three-point line, and the slam dunk contest, and et cetera, et cetera.

jokes.text: Chris: 'Can I ask you a question? Why am I so positive all the time?' Ann: 'Yes, that's exactly the question.' Chris: 'I was born with a blood disorder...'
jokes.setup: Chris asks what seems like a moment of self-reflection
jokes.punchline: Ann assumes it's a genuine rhetorical question, but Chris answers it literally — and with a medical origin story for his positivity
jokes.explanation: Good setup-punchline structure. Ann's 'Yes, that's exactly the question' treats it as rhetorical, but Chris genuinely has an answer ready. The reveal that his positivity has a medical/survival origin is both funny and unexpectedly touching — a hallmark of the show's tone. The misdirection (seems like flirtation, is actually sincere self-disclosure) works well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay Ann, here's what you do. First, wear something that shows you're interested in him. Maybe a nice dress.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then escalate to something a little more daring. A short skirt, maybe some heels.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then a leather jacket. Then a metal bikini. Then a full metal bikini with spikes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By that point he'll either be completely into you or calling animal control.

jokes.text: Leslie is on the phone with Ann, coaching her from outside. When Ann asks why Leslie doesn't just come do it herself, Leslie says 'Okay. Holy crap!' and suddenly appears at the restaurant.
jokes.setup: Leslie is calling Ann to coach her through the date; Ann challenges Leslie to do it herself
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately appears at the restaurant — she was already there watching, so the 'coaching by phone from outside' was always absurd
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Leslie was already in the restaurant is a good physical comedy beat — it recontextualizes the whole phone call as Leslie watching from across the room. Her 'Holy crap!' of fake surprise is great. Rewatch bonus because you realize she was there the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Turkey chili is sexy.

jokes.text: Leslie calls Ann mid-date from outside: 'Jurassic Park. Parks are so great. The Parks Department needs money. I just did it in three moves.'
jokes.setup: Ann says it's hard to steer conversation from favorite movies to Parks budget
jokes.punchline: Leslie demonstrates the 'three moves' with the most tortured logic imaginable: Jurassic Park → Parks → Parks Department needs money
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The 'three moves' logic — Jurassic Park → Parks → Parks Department needs money — is spectacularly bad segue advice delivered with Leslie's characteristic confidence in her own genius. The specific choice of 'Jurassic Park' as the movie is perfect (it even has 'park' in the title, which Leslie exploits). The 'I just did it in three moves' is triumphant and completely deluded. Strong character integration and economy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I'm Chris now. What do you think of my tuxedo vest?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's very... efficient.

jokes.text: Leslie shows up at the bar where Ann and Chris are on their date, pretending it's a coincidence
jokes.setup: Ann told Leslie to just come do the budget pitch herself; Leslie arrives at the bar and pretends to have coincidentally run into them
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately sees through it; Chris is thrilled and invites everyone to join; the 'coincidence' is tissue-thin and Leslie's cover story is embarrassingly bad
jokes.explanation: A standard cringe situation comedy beat. Leslie's inability to be subtle (established joke) plays out in a predictable way. Ben's 'confirming a suspicion' is the best part. Competent but structurally familiar.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm like a vest. I go over everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A vest. It's versatile. You can wear it in any season. And it complements whatever's underneath.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm seducing you with my vest knowledge. Like the Parks Department, I bring added value to your life. I'm essential but also optional, like a vest.

jokes.text: Ben catches Leslie at the restaurant: 'Well, well, well. Ben. What a fun surprise.' Ben: 'That's right, you were coming here tonight on a date. And hey, Leslie is joining you on this wonderfully romantic occasion. How about that?'
jokes.setup: Leslie has crashed Ann and Chris's date; Ben arrives and immediately understands what she's doing
jokes.punchline: Ben's mock-sincere 'How about that?' drips with sarcasm as he calls out exactly what Leslie is doing while maintaining plausible civility
jokes.explanation: A competent irony beat. Ben's 'How about that?' is the right tone — barely-veiled sarcasm that exposes Leslie while maintaining surface politeness. Works as a character beat for early Ben-Leslie tension.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Every date is a good date. Even the bad dates are good dates because you learn something about yourself.

jokes.text: Ben to Leslie: 'They're both so beautiful. They probably just want to see each other naked.'
jokes.setup: Ben is confronting Leslie about her scheme; Leslie claims innocence
jokes.punchline: Ben's explanation for why Chris and Ann are on a date is delivered as clinical observation — 'they probably just want to see each other naked' — with complete matter-of-factness
jokes.explanation: The clinical frankness of Ben's delivery makes the joke work. He's not being crude — he's just applying Occam's razor to human attraction. Good economy. The juxtaposition of 'they're both so beautiful' with the blunt conclusion is a nice deadpan structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Nurses are incredible. They work so hard, they care so much. I think they should be paid like CEOs.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, they should be paid more than CEOs. They should be paid like the CEO of Google.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: No wait, they should be paid like the CEO of Google, plus stock options, plus a private jet, plus naming rights to a country.

jokes.text: Leslie denies any involvement in the date. Ben: 'I know what you're trying to do, and you're not that good at being sneaky.' Leslie: 'Yes, I am.' Ben: 'No, you're not.' Leslie: 'I'm great at being sneaky.' Ben: 'Clearly, you're not.'
jokes.setup: Ben has caught Leslie in the act of crashing the date she arranged
jokes.punchline: Leslie insists she's great at being sneaky while being caught red-handed — the argument itself proves Ben's point
jokes.explanation: Works as a nice irony beat — Leslie arguing for her sneakiness in a situation that definitively disproves it. The back-and-forth is tight and the logic is airtight from Ben's perspective. Good early chemistry between Leslie and Ben.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm not just positive. I have calculated the exact percentage of my life that I have left to live, and I am determined to enjoy every single week of it. By my calculations, I have approximately 2,847 weeks left. That's 40,276 days. So I'm going to enjoy every one of them.

jokes.text: Tom's talking-head: 'Yes, Ron Swanson is dating my ex-wife, Wendy. Big deal. My girlfriend, Lucy, is the sexiest woman in town. She's Cuban, she's got tattoos, and she's into me, which, as far as I'm concerned, is the sexiest quality a woman can have.'
jokes.setup: Tom addresses the awkward situation of Ron dating his ex-wife
jokes.punchline: Tom's bravado crashes into his ultimate criterion for sexiness: that a woman 'is into me' — admitting his deepest insecurity while trying to sound confident
jokes.explanation: The joke builds through Tom's confident catalog of his girlfriend's attributes (Cuban, tattoos) to land on the deeply insecure punchline: the sexiest quality is simply that she's attracted to him. This self-aware vulnerability disguised as braggadocio is great character writing. 'As far as I'm concerned' is the perfect qualifier.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So anyway, like I was saying, the Parks Department is really important and—

dialogue.speaker: Other person
dialogue.line: Yeah, did you see the game last night?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, sports! You know what's like sports? Parks. Parks are a level playing field where everyone can—

jokes.text: Leslie suggests taking a walk by the pond in Ramsett Park after dinner to set up a budget conversation; Ben immediately notes 'Too bad the park's always closed, though.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to engineer a romantic Parks-related moment to pitch Chris on the budget
jokes.punchline: Ben punctures her scheme by pointing out the park is always closed — the very problem they're trying to solve makes Leslie's plan impossible
jokes.explanation: A tight ironic beat — Leslie's romantic Parks pitch is undermined by the exact thing they're fighting against. Ben's flat delivery of the obvious problem is a good straight-man moment. The structural irony is satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: If you want it done right, why don't you just come do it yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I will.

jokes.text: Chris converts the group dinner into a full nightclub outing and declares 'This place is outstanding!' / 'Look, even Ben's dancing.'
jokes.setup: Chris suggests taking the 'date-plus-two-other-people' thing 'up into the stratosphere'
jokes.punchline: The next shot is a nightclub; Ben — the most buttoned-up character — is apparently dancing; Chris announcing it with pride implies Ben's dancing is a spectacle
jokes.explanation: The 'even Ben is dancing' visual gag works because Ben is established as reserved. Chris's delight at this is character-consistent. The visual of Ben dancing is implied comedy we don't see in the transcript but can infer. Competent situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Chris and Ann are totally going to get together.

jokes.text: Tom referees basketball with made-up calls: 'That's a technical difficulty.' / 'Andy's team throws the ball from the stripey thing.'
jokes.setup: Tom is refereeing the basketball game and making calls
jokes.punchline: Tom calls a 'technical difficulty' (merging 'technical foul' with tech support terminology) and refers to the free throw line as 'the stripey thing'
jokes.explanation: 'Technical difficulty' is a great malapropism — sounds close enough to the real term to be plausible from Tom, and the tech-support connotation is funny. 'The stripey thing' as official referee terminology for the free throw line is charmingly ignorant. Both land well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm actually really sneaky. I'm like a ninja.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, you're wearing a neon green jacket that says 'Parks Department' on the back.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's my disguise.

jokes.text: Tom's basketball refereeing: 'That's a technical difficulty.' 'So, that means Andy's team throws the ball from the stripey thing.'
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to referee basketball using made-up terminology
jokes.punchline: 'Technical difficulty' instead of 'technical foul,' and 'the stripey thing' instead of 'the free throw line'
jokes.explanation: 'Technical difficulty' is a great malapropism — close enough to be understandable, wrong enough to be absurd. 'The stripey thing' is even better: Tom abandons official terminology altogether and just describes what he sees, as if he has no prior knowledge of basketball courts. Both are strong, specific word choices.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you're dating my ex-wife? That's cool. I mean, it's a little weird, but it's cool.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Actually, it's pretty weird.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, it's really weird.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, you're dating my ex-wife. Do you understand what you're doing to me? I'm the one who has to see you two together.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm the victim here.

jokes.text: Chris buys a drink for the man who tried to hit on Ann, saying 'Let me buy all of you a drink for being so welcoming today' and then calls out 'Waiter!'
jokes.setup: A man hits on Ann at the bar; Chris introduces Ann as his date
jokes.punchline: Rather than being territorial or awkward, Chris thanks the man for being 'so welcoming' and buys everyone drinks — his positivity is so extreme he rewards a rival for trying to steal his date
jokes.explanation: Chris's extreme positivity expressed through rewarding a potential romantic rival is a great character beat. 'For being so welcoming today' is the funny framing — as if the man who hit on his date was performing community service. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could take a romantic walk through the park this weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Actually, all the parks are closed due to budget cuts.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's... we have to do something about this.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I know. It's devastating.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking-head: 'I'm sort of a gay hero. Last year, I married two penguins at the zoo, and it turned out they were both gay. Penguin wedding? That's cute. It was so cute.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is explaining why she's celebrated at the bar (drinks are on the house)
jokes.punchline: She accidentally officiated a gay penguin wedding at the zoo and now considers herself a hero of LGBTQ+ rights; the repeated 'It was so cute' is the perfect Leslie emotional response
jokes.explanation: A delightful joke with multiple layers. Leslie accidentally officiating a gay penguin wedding and then self-designating as a 'gay hero' is absurd and charming. The detail that she 'didn't know they were both gay' at the time makes it accidental heroism. 'It was so cute' as her deepest civic takeaway is perfect Leslie. Original enough to earn a strong score.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: This is literally the most incredible club I've ever been to in my entire life. The lighting design, the energy, the way the bass frequencies resonate through your thoracic cavity — it's a perfect ten out of ten. Actually, I'd say it's an eleven out of ten. No, a twelve. The DJ is phenomenal, the crowd is enthusiastic, and I'm having the time of my life right now. This might be the best night ever!

jokes.text: Ben reveals his backstory: 'When I was 18 and I became mayor of my hometown... I used every last dollar we had to open a giant winter sports complex. Called it Ice Town. And it turned out great and everyone loved it.' [Pause] 'Yeah, kind of. It was never completed, and I got impeached.'
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining why he's cautious about spending money on big projects like the Parks budget
jokes.punchline: He starts to tell the story positively ('turned out great, everyone loved it'), then immediately corrects with the devastating truth: it was never completed and he got impeached at age 18
jokes.explanation: A great character revelation with excellent structure. The bait-and-switch ('turned out great and everyone loved it' → 'it was never completed, and I got impeached') is well-timed. Getting impeached at 18 for an unfinished winter sports complex explains Ben's entire cautious personality in one sentence. Strong economy, strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, that's traveling. No wait, that's a foul. Actually, that's a technical foul. And now he's in violation of the Magna Carta.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't know, I'm just making stuff up now. That guy just committed... high treason against the sport of basketball.

jokes.text: Ben's Ice Town backstory: 'When I was 18 and I became mayor of my hometown, I used every last dollar we had to open a giant winter sports complex. Called it Ice Town. And it turned out great and everyone loved it.' [beat] 'Yeah, kind of. It was never completed, and I got impeached.'
jokes.setup: Ben is responding to Leslie's accusation that he doesn't take chances
jokes.punchline: Ben starts with a positive spin on Ice Town ('turned out great, everyone loved it'), then immediately corrects himself: never completed, impeached
jokes.explanation: Excellent backstory reveal. The structure is perfect: positive framing, then immediate self-correction. 'Got impeached' at 18 years old is a tremendous amount of civic failure to pack into one sentence. It works as character establishment for Ben (risk-averse precisely because of this experience) and as a standalone joke. Rewatch bonus because Ice Town becomes a running gag throughout the series.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: That's a foul. No wait, the guy on the stripey thing is open.

jokes.text: The newspaper headline about Ben: 'Ice Town Costs Ice Clown His Town Crown.' 'They were big into rhymes.'
jokes.setup: Ben describes getting impeached over Ice Town
jokes.punchline: The headline is a perfectly structured rhyme: 'Ice Town Costs Ice Clown His Town Crown' — and Ben's resigned explanation that 'they were big into rhymes' is the deadpan kicker
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. 'Ice Town Costs Ice Clown His Town Crown' is a masterwork of internal rhyme and alliteration — it would be impressive as a standalone joke, but delivered as a newspaper headline that defined Ben's adolescence and explains his entire personality, it's exceptional. The addition of 'They were big into rhymes' is the perfect kicker: Ben's resigned acceptance, the implication of a small-town paper's editorial style, and the understatement of his humiliation. This is the kind of line that gets quoted for years. Economy is near-perfect. Earns 9.0 — comparable to the anchor examples.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I'm basically a gay hero. I once accidentally married two gay penguins at the zoo.

jokes.text: Tom's refereeing escalation: ejecting players for 'taking a number two on number four,' 'roughing the passer,' 'double dribbling,' and 'touching the basketball'
jokes.setup: The basketball game grows chaotic; Tom is refereeing and making calls
jokes.punchline: Tom's calls escalate from vaguely basketball-adjacent to completely made-up ('touching the basketball' is a foul?) while mixing in football terminology
jokes.explanation: The escalating absurdity of Tom's made-up calls — culminating in fouling someone for 'touching the basketball' — is a solid sustained bit. 'Taking a number two on number four' is the best specific call. The cumulative effect is funnier than any individual element.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ice Town was a great success. We had Ice Rinks, Ice Sculptures, the Ice Skating Lottery...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Sure, we went bankrupt and had to lay off half the staff, but we really captured the magic of ice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, fine, it was a disaster. A complete disaster. I cost the town millions of dollars and everyone hates me.

jokes.text: Ron attempts to pull Tom's referee shirt off him; Tom ejects Ron. 'I'm ejecting you. You're ejected, too. Everyone's ejected.' Including a random spectator woman.
jokes.setup: Ron confronts Tom over his refereeing; Tom ejects Ron
jokes.punchline: Tom's ejection power goes to his head and he begins ejecting everyone — players, coaches, bystanders — including a spectator woman who presumably did nothing wrong
jokes.explanation: Tom's power trip as referee is a good escalation beat. The random woman being ejected is the best specific joke within the sequence — collateral damage from Tom's ego. Ron's physical confrontation with Tom adds to the chaos. Good energy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: They're calling it 'Ben's Lyin' and Tryin'.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Which is ridiculous because those words don't even rhyme.

jokes.text: Andy wins by forfeit and dedicates the victory to April: 'I dedicate this victory to April Ludgate. It feels good. And it feels sticky. From the Gatorade.'
jokes.setup: Andy's team wins by forfeit amid the referee chaos; Andy gives a victory speech
jokes.punchline: Andy's emotional dedication to April is immediately undercut by the mundane clarification that the stickiness he's feeling is from Gatorade — he felt the need to specify
jokes.explanation: The two-part punchline works well: emotional dedication to April (sweet) followed by the physical clarification about Gatorade stickiness (grounding and funny). Andy specifying the source of the stickiness implies an awareness of how that sentence sounds — but delivered with no irony. Perfect Andy voice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Number 23, that's a solid player. Number 24? Also great. But Number 25? That guy's all clogged up.

jokes.text: Leslie tries to claim the Ann/Chris date was 'both of our ideas but mostly Ann's' before admitting she engineered it entirely to get budget money from Chris
jokes.setup: Chris compliments Leslie on arranging the date; Leslie tries to deflect credit
jokes.punchline: Leslie's attempt to give Ann credit unravels in real time until she has fully confessed the entire scheme to Chris
jokes.explanation: A good cringe beat as Leslie's scheme unravels through her own honesty compulsion. The escalating confession is a reliable Leslie comedic device. The delivery matters more than the writing here.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, that was a foul!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That was a clean play, Haverford.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm the ref now, and I say it's a foul. Technical foul. That's two shots.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You can't just make up rules—

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh, I can't? Ejected. You're out of the game.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And you—ejected. And you—ejected. Everyone's ejected. Game's over. I win.

jokes.text: Chris's reaction to learning the date was a scheme to get budget money: 'Wow.' [long pause] 'I've just had my first bad date.' / 'Not that sneaky.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has fully confessed the scheme; Chris absorbs the news
jokes.punchline: Chris's 'I've just had my first bad date' is a callback to his earlier declaration that all dates are 'great or phenomenally great' — the pause before it lands beautifully; Ann's 'Not that sneaky' echoes Ben's earlier note to Leslie
jokes.explanation: An outstanding callback payoff. Chris said he had never had a bad date — all were 'great or phenomenally great.' The revelation of the scheme gives him his first bad date, and his delivery of 'I've just had my first bad date' with appropriate gravity closes the loop perfectly. The pause before the line is a crucial structural element. Ann's added 'Not that sneaky' also callbacks Ben's earlier observation about Leslie. This is how callbacks should work — the payoff is earned and emotionally resonant while still being funny. Earns 8.6.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You're out! You're out of here!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And you, sir, are accused of molesting the ref. Get out!

jokes.text: April's absence explained: 'I was in Venezuela.' Andy: 'Wow. Across the pond.' (Venezuela is not across a pond from Indiana; it's across an ocean and most of South America)
jokes.setup: Andy is reacting to learning April was in Venezuela all summer
jokes.punchline: 'Across the pond' is a British idiom for crossing the Atlantic, and even then it refers to the UK — not Venezuela, which is much farther
jokes.explanation: Three words that reveal Andy has a complete misunderstanding of geography and idioms simultaneously. 'Across the pond' misapplied to Venezuela is the kind of specific intellectual error that reveals Andy's worldview. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I want to dedicate this victory to April, the love of my life.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You're so beautiful, and you smell like a sweet flower... mixed with something else. What is that?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Gatorade. I've been drinking it all day and it's all over my hands.

jokes.text: Andy meets April's new boyfriend Eduardo; Eduardo says something in Spanish and April translates: 'That means we're going to lunch.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just apologized to April and is blindsided by her having a new boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Eduardo's dramatic-sounding Spanish is translated by April as simply 'we're going to lunch' — deflating the tension with mundane reality
jokes.explanation: A good deflation joke. The implication that dramatic romantic Spanish equates to 'lunch plans' undercuts Andy's emotional moment. April's flat translation is perfectly in her register. Good use of the language barrier for comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I want you to know that this was all Chris's idea. I was completely against it from the start.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: What? No, you came up with this!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Chris is obviously confused. Ann, you know how he gets.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, I was literally in the room when you planned this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann's been under a lot of stress lately. I think she might be misremembering things.

jokes.text: Andy asks: 'How do you say "Have a great time, don't choke on anything"?' as April and Eduardo leave
jokes.setup: Andy has just been devastated by meeting April's boyfriend; he needs to say goodbye
jokes.punchline: Andy's farewell wish — 'have a great time, don't choke on anything' — is simultaneously sweet, passive-aggressive, and so specifically weird that it's clearly just Andy being Andy
jokes.explanation: A quietly excellent joke. 'Don't choke on anything' is Andy's attempt at a farewell wish — it's either a sincere safety concern (very Andy) or a barely concealed hostile wish (also very Andy). The ambiguity between genuine kindness and inadvertent aggression is perfect for the character. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Wait, so you were just using me to get to Ben?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: What? No, Chris, I—

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I can't believe this. My first real date and it was all a setup. This is worse than when I tried to eat that entire rotisserie chicken at the Sweetums office party.

jokes.text: Leslie's idea binder entry: 'Budget solution number 28. Use grazing sheep to mow grass in parks. Note. Tired sheep could become food or sweaters.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is reviewing her budget solutions brainstorm
jokes.punchline: The sheep-as-lawnmowers plan escalates to the note that tired sheep 'could become food or sweaters' — revealing Leslie has thought through the entire sheep life cycle as a budget solution
jokes.explanation: The sheep plan is funny, but the 'Note' addition about tired sheep becoming food or sweaters reveals Leslie's systematic thinking applied to an absurd problem. The 'or sweaters' is the key detail — she's thought through both outcomes and noted them for completeness. Very much in Leslie's organized, overcommitted character voice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I was in Venezuela.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Venezuela? Isn't that across the pond?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, Andy. It's in South America.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh. I thought it was near England or something.

jokes.text: Leslie's pep talk to Andy: 'When your back's against the wall and odds are stacked against you, you just... You swing the hardest, damn it. You go big or you go home.' Andy: 'I'm not. I don't even really have a home.'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers an inspirational speech about going after what you want
jokes.punchline: Leslie ends with 'you don't seem like the kind of guy who goes home'; Andy clarifies he literally doesn't have a home — deflating the metaphor with his actual homeless status
jokes.explanation: A very effective misdirection joke. Leslie's motivational cliché ('you don't seem like the guy who goes home') is literalized by Andy's actual homelessness — the abstract metaphor crashes into concrete reality. The specificity that Andy literally has no home (established character fact) makes this a character-integrated joke rather than a generic subversion. Strong structure.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: This is my boyfriend, Eduardo.

dialogue.speaker: Eduardo
dialogue.line: We're not dating.

jokes.text: Leslie's big pitch includes: 'Check your testicles? No. Not that. Although that is very good advice. Looking at you, Jerry.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is building to her big idea to save the department; asks the team what the answer could be
jokes.punchline: Someone (or Leslie herself) suggests 'check your testicles'; Leslie rejects it but affirms it's 'very good advice,' then specifically calls out Jerry to check his — with no explanation for why Jerry specifically needs this reminder
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of 'check your testicles' as a department-saving idea, and Leslie's sincere endorsement of it as 'very good advice' before singling out Jerry. The 'looking at you, Jerry' is the best element — the specific targeting of Jerry for this advice, with zero context provided, is funnier than any explanation would be.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Adiós. I'm leaving now. Adiós, amigos.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: May your socks never get wet, and may you always find twenty dollars in your old jacket.

jokes.text: Leslie's Harvest Festival pitch includes: 'People from all over Indiana would come and gaze in wonderment at how fat our citizens were. And while they were here, they would also attend the Festival.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is pitching the Harvest Festival as historically known for two things
jokes.punchline: The first thing Pawnee was historically known for is 'widespread obesity' — and this is presented as a draw, with tourists coming to gaze at the citizens, and the Festival being secondary
jokes.explanation: Pawnee's obesity as a legitimate tourist attraction — where people would 'gaze in wonderment' at the citizens — is a darkly funny bit of civic pride. Leslie presents this as a selling point without irony. The structure (two things → obesity first, festival second) inverts expected priorities well. Good Pawnee world-building comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We could use tired sheep for food or sweaters.

jokes.text: Chris's reaction to Leslie's speech: 'That, literally, is the most moving thing I've ever heard.' [pause] 'And a good idea.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has given an emotional, passionate speech about the Parks Department's purpose
jokes.punchline: Chris is moved to the point where he has to add 'and a good idea' as an afterthought — as if he was so swept up in the emotion he nearly forgot to evaluate it professionally
jokes.explanation: The pause between 'the most moving thing I've ever heard' and 'And a good idea' is the joke — Chris was so emotionally overwhelmed he needed a beat to remember he's a policy professional. The afterthought quality of 'and a good idea' is perfect understatement. Good character beat for Chris.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thinking Venezuela is a city in Mexico

jokes.text: Leslie announces: 'Okay. So, everybody, we're going to party hard for 15 minutes and then, we're going to have our first brainstorming session.'
jokes.setup: The team celebrates their plan being approved
jokes.punchline: Leslie time-limits the celebration to exactly 15 minutes, then immediately schedules productive work — she can't even celebrate without a plan
jokes.explanation: A compact character joke: Leslie schedules joy. 'Party hard for 15 minutes' followed by the immediate pivot to brainstorming is quintessential Leslie — even her celebration is organized. The specificity of '15 minutes' is funnier than any vaguer timeframe would be.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You need to believe in yourself. You need to have confidence that you can achieve anything you set your mind to.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I don't have a home.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, that's not what I meant—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I've been living in a tent behind the community center for three weeks.

jokes.text: Andy goes to April with flowers to declare his pursuit: 'I like April. And I'm coming after her with everything I've got.' Then asks her out. She says no. Andy: 'I thought you were going to say yes. But that's okay.'
jokes.setup: Andy confronts April with romantic intentions despite her having a boyfriend present
jokes.punchline: April says no; Andy's response is to acknowledge he expected yes and then immediately pivot to 'but that's okay' — not missing a beat in his pursuit
jokes.explanation: Andy's confident prediction ('I thought you were going to say yes') being immediately wrong, and his total equanimity about it, is a good Andy joke. The gap between his confident expectation and reality — met with cheerful persistence — is the core Andy Dwyer comedic engine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, the point is that you have to believe in yourself. You have to think positive thoughts and—

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Say no more. I'm going to go tell everyone that I'm the best dancer in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not... okay. Also, Jerry, you need to go check your testicles.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just... go do it.

jokes.text: Andy commits to asking April out every day: 'I'll be back tomorrow to ask you again. And again the next day. And the next day. Not Friday. I have to go visit my cousin. But I will be back after that to ask you again.'
jokes.setup: Andy is vowing to persistently pursue April despite rejection
jokes.punchline: The romantic declaration of daily pursuit is interrupted by the specific exception of Friday — he has to visit his cousin — which both deflates the grand gesture and somehow makes it more endearing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a great final beat for the Andy/April storyline. The structure is nearly perfect: the romantic declaration escalates ('tomorrow, and the next day, and the next day') and then the Friday exception crashes it — but the exception is so mundane (cousin visit) and Andy reaffirms his commitment after it so sincerely that the joke has three beats. It's romantic comedy and character comedy simultaneously, and it earns both. The cousin caveat makes Andy more human and funnier. High quotability. Earns 8.5.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Pawnee was founded in 1823 by settlers who were looking for the flattest land possible. We succeeded. We also have the highest obesity rate in the state, and we're very proud of that. And, of course, the Harvest Festival.

jokes.text: Eduardo tells April (in Spanish) to go for it with Andy; April looks shocked and says 'Oh, my God. Really? That's awesome.' then immediately tells Andy 'I'll see you tomorrow.'
jokes.setup: Eduardo has been presented as a romantic rival throughout; the episode has set him up as an obstacle
jokes.punchline: Eduardo encourages April to pursue Andy — the apparent rival is actually the wingman; April's 'Oh, my God. Really? That's awesome' breaks her deadpan; she immediately accepts Andy's implicit date
jokes.explanation: A satisfying misdirection payoff — Eduardo as wingman rather than rival is unexpected and sweet. April's broken deadpan ('Oh, my God. Really? That's awesome') is a rare emotional crack in her armor, which makes it both funny and touching. The rewatch value is high because Eduardo's role is set up as antagonistic. Good structural subversion of the classic rivals plot.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: People specifically came to marvel at obesity

tmdb_overview: Leslie and the Parks Department return to work after three months to discover that the budget crisis still looms. After unsuccessfully trying to have their budget restored by using Ann to charm Chris with a date, Leslie decides to make an all or nothing play by resurrecting the Pawnee Harvest Festival. Meanwhile, Ben restarts the youth basketball league and instates Ron and Andy to coach the only two teams. April returns from a vacation with a new boyfriend.
insight: Season 3 premiere resets with 73 jokes in 24 minutes—character-driven setup over laughs.
